bmt-2016-power-01d.title: Derivative at 1
bmt-2016-power-01d.body:
For every polynomial $q$, $D(q)=2q'(1)-q(1)$ (true on each $x^k$: $2k-1$, and both sides are linear). Hence $D((2x-1)^{10})=2\cdot20(2\cdot1-1)^9-(2\cdot1-1)^{10}=40-1=39$.

**Answer: 39**

bmt-2016-power-02a.title: Counterexample
bmt-2016-power-02a.body:
The function $f:\{\text{animals}\}\to\mathbb R$ sending an animal to its number of legs is a function but not a functional, because its inputs are animals, not functions. (Likewise $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ takes numbers, not functions.)

**Answer: False**

bmt-2016-power-02b.title: By definition
bmt-2016-power-02b.body:
A functional is a function (it maps each element of its domain to a real number) whose domain happens to be a set of functions. Its outputs are real, so it is a real-valued function.

**Answer: True**

bmt-2016-power-02c.title: Counterexample
bmt-2016-power-02c.body:
The functional $\mathrm{Lead}$ (leading coefficient) restricted to the non-constant polynomials has codomain $\mathbb R$, but the real numbers (viewed as constant functions) are not in its domain. The codomain is not contained in the domain.

**Answer: False**

bmt-2016-power-03a.title: Reasons
bmt-2016-power-03a.body: Three reasons: (i) to state a range one must know exactly which values the function achieves, but when a function is just being defined those values may not be known; the codomain only says where values live. (ii) Without a codomain there would be no notion of surjectivity (onto), and isomorphism theorems would weaken; functions into and out of a space need not line up exactly. (iii) It is easier to define a function by what it could be than by what it exactly is.

bmt-2016-power-03b.title: Answer
bmt-2016-power-03b.body: $\mathrm{Lead}$ is not injective: many polynomials share the same leading coefficient, so there is no left inverse (no $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda(\mathrm{Lead}(p))=p$ for all $p$). But right inverses exist: maps $\Lambda$ with $\mathrm{Lead}(\Lambda(c))=c$, e.g. $\Lambda(c)=cx^2$ for $c\ne0$; at $c=0$ the choice is forced to be the zero polynomial, which is fine only as a convention since the zero polynomial has no leading coefficient. So only a partial, one-sided inverse exists, and it is far from unique.

bmt-2016-power-03c.title: Discussion
bmt-2016-power-03c.body:
$\mathrm{Ev}_2(f)$ applies the functional to the function $f$, giving $f(2)=2^y+z$. $\mathrm{Ev}_2(x^y+z)$ literally applies it to an *expression*, not a function; it only makes sense if the expression is understood as shorthand for $x\mapsto x^y+z$, in which case the value is again $2^y+z$. Similarly $\mathrm{Ev}_2(g)=g(2)=6$ and $\mathrm{Ev}_2(x^2+x)$ equals $6$ if read as the function in $x$.

The second abuse is more acceptable, since $x$ is clearly the active variable. In the first, the intended active variable is ambiguous: the expression $x^y+z$ could also be read as the function $z\mapsto x^y+z$ or $y\mapsto x^y+z$ (with different results). The ambiguity can be avoided without naming a function by writing $\mathrm{Ev}_2(x\mapsto x^y+z)$.

bmt-2016-power-04c.title: Proof
bmt-2016-power-04c.body: For $p=x^n$: $\frac{b^{n+1}-a^{n+1}}{n+1}+\frac{c^{n+1}-b^{n+1}}{n+1}=\frac{c^{n+1}-a^{n+1}}{n+1}$. All three functionals are linear, and every polynomial is a linear combination of powers $x^n$, so the identity holds for every polynomial. ∎

bmt-2016-power-05a.title: Compute the integrals over $[-1,1]$
bmt-2016-power-05a.body:
Odd integrands integrate to $0$ over $[-1,1]$ and $\mathrm{Int}[-1,1](x^{2m})=\frac{2}{2m+1}$.

- $\{1,x\}$: $\mathrm{Int}(x)=0$ ✓.
- $\{1,x^2\}$: $\mathrm{Int}(x^2)=\frac23\ne0$ ✗.
- $\{x,x^2\}$: $\mathrm{Int}(x^3)=0$ ✓.
- $\{1,x^2-\frac13\}$: $\frac23-\frac13\cdot2=0$ ✓.
- $\{x^2-1,x^3\}$: product $x^5-x^3$ is odd, integral $0$ ✓.

**Answer: all except $\{1,x^2\}$.**

bmt-2016-power-05b.title: Check each pair
bmt-2016-power-05b.body:
- $\{1,x,x^2\}$ fails since $\mathrm{Int}(1\cdot x^2)=\frac23$.
- $\{1,x,\frac32x^2-\frac12\}$: $\mathrm{Int}(\frac32x^2-\frac12)=1-1=0$; $x\cdot(\ldots)$ is odd. ✓
- $\{1,x^2-1,x^3\}$ fails since $\mathrm{Int}(x^2-1)=\frac23-2\ne0$.
- $\{1,x^2-\frac13,x^3+2x\}$: $\mathrm{Int}(x^2-\frac13)=0$, and $x^3+2x$ is odd, so its products with $1$ and with the even polynomial $x^2-\frac13$ are odd. ✓

**Answer: the second and fourth sets.**

bmt-2016-power-06a.title: Impose the conditions
bmt-2016-power-06a.body: Suppose $ax+b$ works. Orthogonal to $1$: $\mathrm{Int}[-1,1](ax+b)=2b=0$, so $b=0$. Then orthogonality to $x^3+2x$: $\mathrm{Int}[-1,1](a(x^4+2x^2))=a\left(\frac25+\frac43\right)=0$ forces $a=0$. So the only solution is the zero polynomial; no nonzero linear polynomial exists. ∎

bmt-2016-power-06b.title: Use parity
bmt-2016-power-06b.body:
Try $q=x^3+cx$ (odd). It is automatically orthogonal to $1$ and to $x^2-\frac13$ (odd integrands). Orthogonality with $x$: $\mathrm{Int}[-1,1](x^4+cx^2)=\frac25+\frac{2c}3=0$, so $c=-\frac35$. Thus $q=x^3-\frac35x$ works.

**Answer: $x^3-\frac35x$**

bmt-2016-power-07a.title: Proof
bmt-2016-power-07a.body: Let $p$ be symmetric, so $p(x)-p(-x)=0$ for all real $x$. This is a polynomial with infinitely many roots, hence the zero polynomial. But each term $c\,x^k$ of $p$ with $k$ odd contributes $2c\,x^k$ to $p(x)-p(-x)$ and terms with $k$ even contribute $0$, so the odd-degree coefficients of $p$ all vanish. ∎

bmt-2016-power-07b.title: Proof
bmt-2016-power-07b.body: Let $p$ be antisymmetric: $p(x)+p(-x)=0$ for all real $x$, so this polynomial is zero. A term $c\,x^k$ with $k$ even contributes $2c\,x^k$ to $p(x)+p(-x)$ (odd $k$ contribute $0$), so all even-degree coefficients vanish. ∎

bmt-2016-power-07c.title: Proof
bmt-2016-power-07c.body: By the previous part $p$ has only odd-degree terms. For odd $k$, $\mathrm{Int}[-1,1](x^k)=\frac{1^{k+1}-(-1)^{k+1}}{k+1}=0$. By linearity $\mathrm{Int}[-1,1](p)=0$. ∎

bmt-2016-power-08b.title: Induction
bmt-2016-power-08b.body: Claim: every term of $P_n$ has degree of the same parity as $n$. True for $P_0=1$ and $P_1=x$. If true for $P_{k-1}$ and $P_k$ ($k>0$), then $xP_k$ has terms of degree of parity $k+1$ and $P_{k-1}$ has terms of parity $k-1\equiv k+1$, so $P_{k+1}$ (a combination of these) has only terms of parity $k+1$. ∎ In particular $P_n(-x)=(-1)^nP_n(x)$.

bmt-2016-power-08c.title: Parity and direct computation
bmt-2016-power-08c.body:
$P_1$ and $P_3$ are antisymmetric and $P_4$ is symmetric, so $P_4P_1$ and $P_4P_3$ are antisymmetric and have integral $0$ over $[-1,1]$.

$P_0$: $\mathrm{Int}[-1,1](P_4)=\frac{35}{8}\cdot\frac25-\frac{15}4\cdot\frac23+\frac38\cdot2=\frac74-\frac52+\frac34=0$.

$P_2$: $P_4P_2=\frac{105}{16}x^6-\frac{125}{16}x^4+\frac{39}{16}x^2-\frac3{16}$, with integral $\frac{105}{16}\cdot\frac27-\frac{125}{16}\cdot\frac25+\frac{39}{16}\cdot\frac23-\frac3{16}\cdot2=\frac{15}{8}-\frac{25}{8}+\frac{13}8-\frac38=0$. ∎

bmt-2016-power-09b.title: Degree argument
bmt-2016-power-09b.body:
Suppose there were two different representations. Subtracting and combining like terms gives $\sum_{k=0}^mc_kP_k(x)=0$ with some $c_k
e0$; let $m$ be the largest index with $c_m
e0$. Since $P_m$ has degree $m$ and $P_k$ with $k<m$ has degree less than $m$, the left side has degree exactly $m$ (leading term $c_m\,\mathrm{Lead}(P_m)x^m
e0$), so it cannot be the zero polynomial. Contradiction. Hence the representation is unique. ∎

bmt-2016-power-10a.title: Induction
bmt-2016-power-10a.body:
Note $p_n$ is monic of degree $n$ by construction, and $\langle p_k,p_k\rangle>0$ for $p_k\ne0$ (the polynomial $p_k^2w$ is nonnegative and nonzero on $(a,b)$, so its $\mathrm{Int}[a,b]$ is positive by the Mean Value Theorem argument), so the formula is defined. We show $p_0,\dots,p_n$ are pairwise orthogonal by induction on $n$; for $n=0$ there is nothing to show. If $p_0,\dots,p_n$ are pairwise orthogonal then for $m\le n$,
$$\langle p_{n+1},p_m\rangle=\langle x^{n+1},p_m\rangle-\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{\langle x^{n+1},p_k\rangle}{\langle p_k,p_k\rangle}\langle p_k,p_m\rangle=\langle x^{n+1},p_m\rangle-\langle x^{n+1},p_m\rangle=0,$$
since only $k=m$ survives. ∎

bmt-2016-power-10b.title: Existence and uniqueness
bmt-2016-power-10b.body:
Existence: by induction on the degree $d$. A constant is a multiple of $p_0$. If every polynomial of degree $\le d$ is such a sum, take $q$ of degree $d+1$ with leading coefficient $c$; then $q-\frac{c}{\mathrm{Lead}(p_{d+1})}p_{d+1}$ has degree $\le d$ and is such a sum, so $q$ is too.

Uniqueness: if there were two different expressions, subtracting them gives $\sum_{k\le n}c_kp_k=0$ with $c_n\ne0$. But $c_np_n$ has degree $n$ and the other terms have lower degree, so the sum has degree $n$ and is not the zero polynomial. Contradiction. ∎

bmt-2016-power-11a.title: Expand $q$
bmt-2016-power-11a.body: Write $q=\sum_{k}c_kp_k$. The largest index $k$ appearing equals $\deg q<n$ (the degree of the sum is the largest degree present), so $p_n$ does not occur and every $k<n$. By linearity $\langle p_n,q\rangle=\sum c_k\langle p_n,p_k\rangle=0$. ∎

bmt-2016-power-11b.title: Split the interval
bmt-2016-power-11b.body: $p$ has finitely many roots, so choose $a<c<d<b$ such that $p$ has no root in $(c,d)$; there $p>0$. By the Mean Value Theorem $\mathrm{Int}[c,d](p)=(d-c)p(\xi)>0$ for some $\xi\in(c,d)$, and also $\mathrm{Int}[a,c](p)=(c-a)p(\xi')\ge0$, $\mathrm{Int}[d,b](p)\ge0$ (as $p\ge0$ on $(a,b)$). By additivity of $\mathrm{Int}$ over intervals, $\mathrm{Int}[a,b](p)>0$. ∎

bmt-2016-power-11c.title: Sign-change argument
bmt-2016-power-11c.body: Let $r_1,\dots,r_k$ be the roots of $p_n$ in $(a,b)$ of odd multiplicity, and put $q=(x-r_1)\cdots(x-r_k)$ (so $q=1$ if $k=0$). Then $p_nq$ has all its roots of even multiplicity in $(a,b)$, so it does not change sign on $(a,b)$; replacing $q$ by $-q$ if necessary, $p_nqw\ge0$ on $(a,b)$ and it is not the zero polynomial, so $\langle p_n,q\rangle>0$ by (ii). If $k<n$ then $\deg q<n$ and (i) gives $\langle p_n,q\rangle=0$, a contradiction. Hence $k\ge n$; since $p_n$ has degree $n$, $k=n$ and all $n$ roots are real, simple and lie in $(a,b)$. ∎

bmt-2016-power-12a.title: Expand and use orthogonality
bmt-2016-power-12a.body: The left side has no $x^{n+1}$ term, so it has degree at most $n$ and equals $\sum_{j=0}^nc_jp_j$ for some reals $c_j$. For $m<n-1$, take $\langle\cdot,p_m\rangle$: $\langle p_{n+1},p_m\rangle=0$ and $\langle xp_n,p_m\rangle=\langle p_n,xp_m\rangle=0$ because $\deg(xp_m)=m+1<n$. So $c_mh_m=0$, and $c_m=0$ for $m<n-1$. Put $a_n=c_n$, $b_n=c_{n-1}$. ∎

bmt-2016-power-12b.title: Take an inner product with $p_{n-1}$
bmt-2016-power-12b.body:
Take $\langle\cdot,p_{n-1}\rangle$ of both sides. Left: $\langle p_{n+1},p_{n-1}\rangle=0$ and $\langle xp_n,p_{n-1}\rangle=\langle p_n,xp_{n-1}\rangle$. Since $xp_{n-1}=\frac{k_{n-1}}{k_n}p_n+(\text{degree}<n)$, this equals $\frac{k_{n-1}}{k_n}h_n$. Right: $a_n\cdot0+b_nh_{n-1}$. So $-\frac{k_{n+1}}{k_n}\cdot\frac{k_{n-1}}{k_n}h_n=b_nh_{n-1}$, i.e. $b_n=-\dfrac{k_{n-1}k_{n+1}h_n}{k_n^2h_{n-1}}$.

**Answer: $b_n=-\frac{k_{n-1}k_{n+1}h_n}{k_n^2h_{n-1}}$**

bmt-2016-power-13a.title: Roots
bmt-2016-power-13a.body:
No. For orthogonal polynomials, $p_2$ must have two distinct real roots in $(a,b)$, but $x^2$ has only one distinct root ($0$). So $x^2$ cannot belong to any such sequence, for any choice of $a,b,w$.

**Answer: No**

bmt-2016-power-13b.title: Statement
bmt-2016-power-13b.body:
Known result: let $n>k$ and let $r_1<\dots<r_k$ be the roots of $p_k$. Then $p_n$ has a root in each of the $k+1$ open intervals $(a,r_1),(r_1,r_2),\dots,(r_{k-1},r_k),(r_k,b)$. In particular (for $n=k+1$) the $k+1$ roots of $p_{k+1}$ strictly interlace with the $k$ roots of $p_k$; and both polynomials have only simple real roots inside $(a,b)$. Both facts rest on the earlier theorem that $p_n$ has $n$ distinct roots in $(a,b)$.

This is the official statement of the strongest result; no complete proof of the general case is expected here.

bmt-2016-power-14a.title: Coefficients
bmt-2016-power-14a.body:
$\langle x^4,P_0\rangle=\frac25$, $\langle P_0,P_0\rangle=2$, so the $P_0$ coefficient is $\frac15$. $\langle x^4,P_1\rangle=0$. $\langle x^4,P_2\rangle=\frac32\cdot\frac27-\frac12\cdot\frac25=\frac8{35}$ and $\langle P_2,P_2\rangle=\frac25$ (see 14(c)), so the $P_2$ coefficient is $\frac47$. The approximation is $\frac15+\frac47\left(\frac32x^2-\frac12\right)=\frac67x^2-\frac3{35}$.

**Answer: $\frac67x^2-\frac3{35}$**

bmt-2016-power-14b.title: Coefficients
bmt-2016-power-14b.body:
By parity only $P_1,P_3$ contribute. $\langle x^5,P_1\rangle=\frac27$, $\langle P_1,P_1\rangle=\frac23$: coefficient $\frac37$. $\langle x^5,P_3\rangle=\frac52\cdot\frac29-\frac32\cdot\frac27=\frac8{63}$, $\langle P_3,P_3\rangle=\frac27$: coefficient $\frac49$. So the approximation is $\frac37x+\frac49\left(\frac52x^3-\frac32x\right)=\frac{10}9x^3-\frac5{21}x$.

**Answer: $\frac{10}{9}x^3-\frac{5}{21}x$**

bmt-2016-power-14c.title: Induction using the recurrence
bmt-2016-power-14c.body:
Claim: $\langle P_k,P_k\rangle=\frac2{2k+1}$. True for $k=0$ ($\mathrm{Int}[-1,1](1)=2$); also $k=1$: $\frac23$. Let $n\ge1$ and assume the claim for $n$. The recurrence at index $n+1$ reads $P_{n+2}=\frac{2n+3}{n+2}xP_{n+1}-\frac{n+1}{n+2}P_n$, i.e. $xP_{n+1}=\frac{n+2}{2n+3}P_{n+2}+\frac{n+1}{2n+3}P_n$. Using the recurrence for $P_{n+1}$ and orthogonality:
$$\langle P_{n+1},P_{n+1}\rangle=\left\langle P_{n+1},\tfrac{2n+1}{n+1}xP_n-\tfrac n{n+1}P_{n-1}\right\rangle=\tfrac{2n+1}{n+1}\langle xP_{n+1},P_n\rangle=\tfrac{2n+1}{n+1}\cdot\tfrac{n+1}{2n+3}\langle P_n,P_n\rangle=\tfrac{2n+1}{2n+3}\cdot\tfrac2{2n+1}=\tfrac2{2(n+1)+1}.$$
(Here $\langle P_{n+1},P_{n-1}\rangle=0$ and $\langle P_{n+2},P_n\rangle=0$ by orthogonality.) ∎

bmt-2016-power-15a.title: Discussion
bmt-2016-power-15a.body: The Legendre approximation $p$ of degree $n$ to $q$ crosses the graph of $q$ many times (potentially at least $n$ times) and does not reflect its slope or smoothness pointwise. What it does: among all polynomials $f$ of degree at most $n$ it minimizes the squared error $\mathrm{Int}[-1,1]\big((f-q)^2\big)$, i.e. it is the least-squares approximation on $[-1,1]$; so it is a good approximation "on average" over the whole interval.

bmt-2016-power-15b.title: Expand in Legendre polynomials
bmt-2016-power-15b.body: Every polynomial $q$ of degree $n$ can be written $q=\sum_{m=0}^nc_mP_m$ (existence, as in the uniqueness/existence argument for orthogonal polynomials: $P_m$ has degree $m$). Then by orthogonality $\langle q,P_k\rangle=c_k\langle P_k,P_k\rangle$, so $\frac{\langle q,P_k\rangle}{\langle P_k,P_k\rangle}=c_k$ and the degree-$n$ Legendre approximation is $\sum_{k=0}^nc_kP_k=q$. ∎

bmt-2016-power-16b.title: Square the generating function
bmt-2016-power-16b.body:
For $|t|<1$: $\sum_{n\ge0}e^{i(n+1)x}t^n=\frac{e^{ix}}{1-te^{ix}}=\frac{e^{ix}(1-te^{-ix})}{|1-te^{ix}|^2}=\frac{e^{ix}-t}{1-2t\cos x+t^2}$. Taking imaginary parts, $\sum_{n\ge0}\sin((n+1)x)t^n=\frac{\sin x}{1-2t\cos x+t^2}$. For $\sin x\ne0$ divide by $\sin x$:
$$\sum_{n}\frac{\sin((n+1)x)}{\sin x}t^n=\left(\frac1{\sqrt{1-2t\cos x+t^2}}\right)^2=\Big(\sum_kP_k(\cos x)t^k\Big)^2=\sum_n\Big(\sum_{k=0}^nP_k(\cos x)P_{n-k}(\cos x)\Big)t^n.$$
Comparing coefficients of $t^n$ gives the identity for every $x$ with $\sin x\ne0$; both sides are polynomials in $\cos x$ (the left side is $U_n(\cos x)$), so it holds for all $x$ by continuity (or since two polynomials agreeing at infinitely many points agree). ∎
